findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Exclude rebar's own permanent flock files (`rebar-fetch.lock`, `rebar-git-op.lock`) from the 124 lock listing, correct the 'rebar reclaims only index.lock' premise, and have the 124 test assert those files are not named.
evidence: Plan: "A 124 is logged as an ERROR that lists every `*.lock` under the common git dir's top level, `refs/` and `logs/`: rebar reclaims only index.lock"
src/rebar/_store/git_locking.py:251 `_FETCH_COORD_LOCK_NAME = "rebar-fetch.lock"`; :329 `lock_path = os.path.join(common, _FETCH_COORD_LOCK_NAME)`; opened O_CREAT and only closed, never deleted
src/rebar/_store/git_locking.py:166 `_STORE_GIT_LOCK_NAME = "rebar-git-op.lock"`, placed in the tracker git dir (:177)
src/rebar/_store/event_commit_git.py:208-216 `_reclaim_stale_maintenance_lock` also reclaims `objects/maintenance.lock`
findings.finding: The plan's justification for the 124 ERROR, that "rebar reclaims only index.lock", is incomplete, and the scan it designs will always report rebar's own lock files as if git had stranded them. Rebar also reclaims stale `objects/maintenance.lock` (`_reclaim_stale_maintenance_lock`). More importantly, rebar keeps flock files named `*.lock` permanently in the scanned directories: `rebar-fetch.lock` is created in the common git dir's top level and never deleted, and `rebar-git-op.lock` sits in the git dir, which is the common dir for a plain clone. Listing every `*.lock` there will name these files on every timeout, next to the real stranded ref locks the warning means to point out.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (124 ERROR lock listing); Testing ('A 124 test plants .git/HEAD.lock')
scenarios: Reflog expiry times out in production. The ERROR lists `rebar-fetch.lock` (and `rebar-git-op.lock` on a plain clone) together with `HEAD.lock`. An operator deletes them all, including a flock file a live fetcher still has open, or ignores the list because it is always noisy.
findings.suggested_fix: Filter the listing to exclude names starting with `rebar-` (or the module constants `_FETCH_COORD_LOCK_NAME` and `_STORE_GIT_LOCK_NAME`). Reword the premise as 'rebar reclaims only index.lock and objects/maintenance.lock'. In the 124 test, also create `rebar-fetch.lock` and assert the ERROR does not name it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Limit the reflog expiry to the tickets store's own refs (this worktree's HEAD plus the tickets branch and its remote-tracking ref) instead of `--all`, and add a linked-worktree test showing the host checkout's reflogs are untouched.
evidence: Plan: "run `git reflog expire --all` through `run_git_reaped`"
docs/scale-envelope.md:92: "the tickets store is a linked worktree sharing the object DB"
docs/concurrency.md:822: "The tickets store is a **linked worktree sharing the object DB**, written concurrently by many processes"
src/rebar/_store/paths.py StorePaths.git_dir/git_common_dir explicitly handle a linked-worktree tracker
Plan Measurements: "3 refs, HEAD reflog 4.69 MB" (prod standalone clone, not the linked-worktree layout)
findings.finding: `git reflog expire --all` run from the tickets tracker is not limited to the tickets store. The docs say the tickets store is a linked worktree sharing the host repo's refs and object DB. In that layout `--all` processes every reflog in the shared repository: the host's refs/heads/*, refs/remotes/*, refs/stash, and by default (no --single-worktree) every other worktree's HEAD reflog. So after every ticket write, the step locks and rewrites refs that rebar's write lock does not cover. It can race the developer's own git commands (HEAD.lock or refs/heads/<branch>.lock contention). It also silently expires host-repo reflog and stash entries, which goes beyond the stated problem (the tickets store's reflogs). The prod measurement ('3 refs') comes from a standalone clone, so it does not represent this layout.
scenarios: On a dev host where .tickets-tracker is a linked worktree of the source repo, a ticket write expires the developer's main-checkout HEAD reflog and refs/stash entries older than 30/90 days.
A developer's `git commit` in the main checkout fails with 'Unable to create .../HEAD.lock' or 'cannot lock ref' because the rebar step holds that lock at the same moment.
A 124 kill during expiry strands a host-branch ref lock (e.g. refs/heads/main.lock), which blocks the developer's own git work, not just rebar writes.
findings.suggested_fix: Invoke `git reflog expire <refs>` with an explicit list of tickets refs (HEAD of the tracker worktree, refs/heads/tickets, refs/remotes/<remote>/tickets, resolved the same way the store already names its branch/remote) rather than `--all`. Add a test that builds a host repo plus a linked tickets worktree, ages a host-branch reflog entry, runs run_auto_maintenance on the tracker, and asserts the host entry survives.

findings.finding: The plan does not say how to resume or clean up if the manual reclaim is interrupted. The run takes ~605 s, holds the write lock, and runs by hand over SSM inside the live container. If the session drops or the container restarts mid-gc, git can leave `gc.pid`, `packed-refs.lock` or ref `*.lock` files behind. The plan itself notes that rebar reclaims only index.lock and that a stranded ref lock blocks writes until removed. The runbook gives no check for leftovers, no safe-to-re-run statement, and no cleanup steps.

An operator re-runs the gc after an interruption and it refuses to start because of a stale `gc.pid`, with no documented next step.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the 124 lock listing walk `refs/` and `logs/` recursively, and include the tracker's per-worktree git dir (HEAD.lock, logs/HEAD.lock, logs/**) as well as the common dir. Add a 124 test on a linked-worktree store that plants a per-worktree HEAD.lock and a nested `refs/heads/<b>.lock` and asserts both are named.
evidence: Plan: "lists every `*.lock` under the common git dir's top level, `refs/` and `logs/`"
src/rebar/_commands/init.py:301/320/338/360 create the tracker via `git worktree add`, so HEAD and logs/HEAD live in the per-worktree git dir.
src/rebar/_store/git_locking.py:260 `_resolve_common_git_dir` deliberately follows `commondir` past the per-worktree git dir.
Branch ref and reflog locks are nested paths (refs/heads/<b>.lock, logs/refs/heads/<b>.lock), not top-level entries of refs/ or logs/.
Production (infra/scripts/mcp-entrypoint.sh:173) is a plain clone, so the planted-`.git/HEAD.lock` test covers only the clone layout.
Evidence class: Partially-verified. The git lock-placement behaviour is known, but the plan names no worktree-layout probe.
findings.finding: The 124-timeout ERROR diagnostic lists `*.lock` only under the COMMON git dir's top level, `refs/` and `logs/`. It does not say the walk is recursive, and it skips the per-worktree git dir. `git reflog expire --all` locks the HEAD and reflog files of every worktree, plus nested per-ref locks. Stores created by `rebar init` are linked worktrees, so a stranded `.git/worktrees/<name>/HEAD.lock` or `logs/HEAD.lock`, or a nested `refs/heads/<branch>.lock`, would not be named. Those are the locks most likely stranded by killing a reflog expiry.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (124 ERROR lock listing); Testing ('A 124 test plants `.git/HEAD.lock`')
scenarios: A dev or worktree store's reflog expiry is killed at 30 s while holding `.git/worktrees/tickets/HEAD.lock`. The ERROR lists nothing, the operator sees no culprit, and writes stay blocked.
A kill strands `refs/heads/tickets.lock`. A non-recursive scan of `refs/` misses it.
findings.suggested_fix: Resolve both the tracker git dir (`_resolve_tracker_git_dir`) and the common dir (`_resolve_common_git_dir`). For each, list top-level `*.lock` plus `refs/**/*.lock` and `logs/**/*.lock` (os.walk), de-duplicate, and include the full paths in the ERROR.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Re-run the runbook's cruft-gc verification (old unreachable loose and packed objects removed, a fresh one kept) on git 2.47.3, e.g. in the MCP image. evidence: Plan: "Verified locally on git 2.56: a 30-day-old unreachable loose object and packed object were both removed, a fresh one kept."
Plan: "the production MCP container runs 2.47.3 (measured 2026-11-12), where an unknown task fails the whole `maintenance run`"

Evidence class: Partially-verified. The flags and behaviour were observed on 2.56; the 2.47.3 target is unprobed.
findings.finding: The runbook's reclaim command `git -c pack.threads=1 gc --cruft --prune=2.weeks.ago` is described as "Verified locally on git 2.56", but it is meant to run in the production MCP container on git 2.47.3. The plan itself shows that git-version differences decide feasibility here (the reflog-expire task). The only quoted production timing (605.6 s) is for a full repack, not this cruft gc, which also walks reachability, writes a cruft pack and expires reflogs while holding the write lock.
scenarios: An operator runs the runbook on 2.47.3 and the packed-unreachable removal or prune behaviour differs from the 2.56 check, so the reclaim silently removes less than the runbook's re-measurement expects.
The cruft gc runs much longer than 605.6 s under the write lock, so the 'quiet window' is too short and more writes fail with lock timeouts than planned.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the write_lock acquire timeout and confirm it is ≥ maintenance bound + 30 s, or size the reflog timeout so the total stays within it.
evidence: "so the worst-case lock hold is the maintenance bound plus 30 s"
Runbook bullet: "writes in that window fail with a lock timeout"
findings.finding: Approach step 1 makes the worst-case lock hold 'the maintenance bound plus 30 s', which is about 150 s instead of 120 s. The plan never states the writers' lock-acquire timeout or shows it still exceeds the new worst case. The runbook confirms writers fail with a lock timeout while the lock is held.
scenarios: The write-lock acquire timeout lies between 120 s and 150 s. A slow-but-not-timed-out maintenance plus a slow reflog expiry makes concurrent ticket writes fail where they previously succeeded.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State a default reclaim threshold in the runbook (e.g. unreachable upper bound above N objects or X% of total).
evidence: "Reclaim only when material."
findings.finding: The runbook says 'Reclaim only when material' without defining a threshold. Each operator would have to decide when the 605 s write-blocking reclaim is worth running.
scenarios: One operator reclaims at 200 unreachable objects and takes a 10-minute write outage for nothing; another never reclaims.
findings.suggested_fix: State a default such as: 'reclaim when the unreachable upper bound exceeds 1% of total objects (≈10,000 today), i.e. far above the measured ~157 per 2.5 months.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Give the exact command that holds write_lock around the gc (e.g. a `python -c` wrapper), and state that write_lock has no stale-break or hold cap shorter than the ~605 s gc.
evidence: "Run inside the live MCP container under `rebar._store.lock.write_lock`"
"Full repack, 605.6 s measured"
findings.finding: The runbook says to run gc 'under `rebar._store.lock.write_lock`' but gives no concrete invocation for taking that lock from a shell in the container. It also does not establish that the lock tolerates a ~605 s hold. If the lock implementation breaks stale holders or caps hold time, a concurrent writer could proceed during gc.
scenarios: The operator improvises a lock wrapper incorrectly, or the lock's stale-detection reclaims it mid-gc. A ticket write then races a full repack and prune.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that no rebar code or procedure reads reflog entries older than 30/90 days, and add a one-time `.git/logs` snapshot before the first deployed run (or explicitly justify skipping it).
evidence: "Reflog entries: expired inside the existing write-locked maintenance step"
"HEAD reflog 4.69 MB / 25,933 entries"
findings.finding: Reflog expiry is destructive and irreversible. Its first production run deletes the older part of a 25,933-entry HEAD reflog. The plan justifies the growth trade-off but does not say whether any rebar code path, debugging practice or recovery procedure relies on old reflog entries. It also offers no back-out, such as snapshotting `.git/logs` before the first deployed run.
scenarios: After deploy, someone needs a months-old HEAD reflog entry to reconstruct a failed write. It is gone, and reverting the code cannot restore it.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the ticket records the commit SHA/Gerrit change, the `make verify` exit status (0) and a run timestamp as the attestation.
evidence: "exit status and log live outside the repository"
findings.finding: The [non-codebase] `make verify` AC names its provenance but not the attestation to record on the ticket, such as the pushed commit SHA or change id, the exit status and a timestamp. Without that, completion evidence is unspecified.
scenarios: The AC is marked done with no traceable link between the verify run and the reviewed commit.
findings.suggested_fix: Append to the AC: 'attested on the ticket with the pushed commit SHA / Gerrit change number, exit status 0, and run timestamp.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a failure-disposition statement per arm: reflog-expiry failure = non-fatal, swallowed, maintenance result returned. For a stranded-ref-lock write failure after a kill, state the disposition write callers surface (permanent/needs-operator, not retryable) and point to the operator remedy.
evidence: "rebar reclaims only index.lock, so a ref lock stranded by the kill blocks writes until removed"
"Any failure ... is logged as a warning and never raised."
findings.finding: The plan states that failures of the new reflog-expiry arm are swallowed ('never raised'). It gives no disposition for the failure mode it creates. A reflog expire killed at 30 s can strand a ref/log lock, which 'blocks writes until removed'. The plan does not say what later write callers surface: a lock timeout presented as retryable/WAIT_AND_RETRY, or a permanent NEEDS_INVESTIGATION-style failure. A stranded lock never clears on retry, so a retryable disposition would mislead callers into retrying indefinitely.
scenarios: The reflog expire is killed at 30 s while holding refs/heads/main.lock. Every later ticket write fails, and agents treat it as transient and retry forever until an operator deletes the lock.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Document in the runbook and in docs/scale-envelope.md that expiry is irreversible and that setting `gc.reflogExpire=never` / `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable=never` in the store's repo config disables it without a redeploy; note the code revert as the full rollback.
evidence: "No config key, env var or flag."
Testing: "With `gc.reflogExpire=never` and `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable=never` set in the repo, every entry survives"
No rollback/disable statement for the reflog-expiry behavior.
findings.finding: The change takes effect in production on the first maintenance run after deploy, with no flag by design, and reflog expiry is irreversible: reverting the code does not restore expired entries. The plan states no rollback or disable path. The repository's own `gc.reflogExpire*=never` setting is proven by a test to govern, so it is a de-facto per-store kill switch, but the plan never documents it as the operator's way to stop expiry.
scenarios: After deploy, an operator wants to keep older HEAD reflog entries for an investigation, but no documented way exists to halt expiry short of a code revert, which comes too late for already-expired entries.

Once reflog expiry is added, that sentence is false, and it will contradict the rewritten caveat.
scenarios: A reader of concurrency.md is told the step runs 'only' the incremental tasks and does not know it also expires reflogs and can hold the lock up to 30 s longer.
findings.suggested_fix: In Approach 3, name both the caveat and the 'Scale-up posture' paragraph of docs/concurrency.md. Reword the latter to: 'The explicit step runs git's incremental tasks (commit-graph, loose-objects, incremental-repack), then `git reflog expire --all` under its own 30 s bound; none walks reachability…'.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In infra/runbooks/tickets-store-prune.md, before the gc, list dangling ticket commits (`git fsck --no-reflogs` filtered by the ticket-commit subject pattern), and recover them or confirm none matter. Take a restorable backup (e.g. a copy of `objects/pack` plus loose objects, or `git bundle` of the dangling SHAs), and replace "no rollback needed" with the restore procedure. Add a `DATA LOSS RISK` note.
evidence: Plan: "Nothing ever prunes unreachable objects, such as the leftovers of failed writes, abandoned merges and compaction."
Plan: "Reclaim with `git -c pack.threads=1 gc --cruft --prune=2.weeks.ago` ... Verify by re-measuring; no rollback needed."

src/rebar/_commands/fsck_recover.py:283-311: `fsck_out = _git(tracker_dir, "fsck", "--no-reflogs")` ... collects `dangling commit` SHAs whose subject matches _TICKET_COMMIT_RE and cherry-picks them as recovery.
The runbook has no pre-prune step that lists dangling ticket commits or takes a backup (e.g. `git bundle` / pack copy).
findings.finding: The runbook's reclaim permanently deletes unreachable objects older than 2 weeks, and the plan says "no rollback needed". But rebar's own recovery path depends on those objects. `rebar fsck` recover scans `git fsck --no-reflogs` for dangling ticket commits (the leftovers of failed writes and abandoned merges) and cherry-picks them back. The plan never checks whether any dangling ticket commits are still unrecovered before pruning, and takes no backup. A prune can therefore destroy the only remaining copy of a ticket write that failed but was never recovered.
findings.location: Approach step 2 — infra/runbooks/tickets-store-prune.md ("Verify by re-measuring; no rollback needed")
scenarios: A write fails mid-rebase. Its commit is left dangling and not noticed for more than 2 weeks. The operator runs the runbook and the commit is pruned, so a later `fsck` recover finds "No dangling ticket commits found" and the ticket data is lost for good.
Reflog expiry (now automatic) drops the last reflog reference to an abandoned commit after 30 days. The next runbook gc then deletes it with no warning.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a pre-reclaim gate to the runbook. (1) Run `git fsck --no-reflogs`, keep only the `dangling commit` lines whose subject matches the ticket-commit pattern, and stop to run `rebar fsck` recover if any are unrecovered. (2) Back up the dangling objects, e.g. `git bundle create` with refs pointing at each dangling SHA, or a copy of `.git/objects`, kept until the re-measure is verified. (3) Document how to restore from that backup instead of saying "no rollback needed".

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the *.lock listing recurses under refs/ and logs/ (top level non-recursive), and add a test planting a nested lock (e.g. refs/heads/main.lock) that asserts the ERROR names it.
evidence: "lists every `*.lock` under the common git dir's top level, `refs/` and `logs/`"
"A 124 test plants `.git/HEAD.lock` and asserts the error names it."
findings.finding: The 124 lock enumeration covers 'the common git dir's top level, `refs/` and `logs/`', but the plan does not say whether the search is recursive. Branch ref and reflog locks live in nested paths such as refs/heads/main.lock and logs/refs/heads/main.lock. The only planned test plants a top-level .git/HEAD.lock, so a non-recursive implementation would pass while missing the locks a reflog kill most likely strands.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (lock listing) and Testing (124 HEAD.lock test)
scenarios: The reflog expire is killed while locking refs/heads/main. A non-recursive listing reports no locks, and the operator does not know which file to remove.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a recursive glob over refs/ and logs/ plus a top-level-only glob, and extend the 124 test to plant both .git/HEAD.lock and .git/refs/heads/<branch>.lock.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that the lock listing fires on the reflog call's 124 (say whether maintenance 124 too), scans refs/ and logs/ recursively, and add a test planting a nested refs/heads/<x>.lock; cover this in AC3.
evidence: "lists every `*.lock` under the common git dir's top level, `refs/` and `logs/`"
"A 124 test plants `.git/HEAD.lock` and asserts the error names it."
AC3: "A failing, erroring or timed-out reflog expiry is logged and never raised"
findings.finding: The lock-listing ERROR on a 124 is a specified behavior, but no AC covers it (AC3 says only 'logged and never raised'). Three details are also ambiguous. (a) The bullet does not say whether the listing fires on the reflog's own 124 only, or also when maintenance returns 124. A killed maintenance can strand locks under objects/, which the listed dirs exclude. (b) It does not say whether `refs/` and `logs/` are searched recursively; ref locks live at e.g. refs/heads/main.lock. (c) The 124 test plants only a top-level `.git/HEAD.lock`, so a non-recursive scan would pass it while missing nested ref locks.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (124 ERROR) / Testing ('A 124 test plants .git/HEAD.lock') / AC3
scenarios: A reflog expire killed while updating refs/heads/x stalls writes on refs/heads/x.lock. A flat scan of refs/ never names it, yet the test is green.
findings.suggested_fix: Approach: 'On the reflog call returning 124, log ERROR listing every *.lock at the common git dir top level and recursively under refs/ and logs/.' Testing: also plant `.git/refs/heads/main.lock` and `.git/logs/refs/heads/main.lock` and assert both are named. AC3: append 'and a timed-out expiry's ERROR names stranded lock files.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend the 124 lock scan to the per-worktree git dir (its top level and logs/) as well as the common dir, and add a linked-worktree variant of the 124 test that plants the worktree's HEAD.lock.
evidence: Plan: "lists every `*.lock` under the common git dir's top level, `refs/` and `logs/`"
docs/concurrency.md:821-822: "The tickets store is a **linked worktree sharing the object DB**"; docs/scale-envelope.md:92-93: "the tickets store is a linked worktree sharing the object DB"
src/rebar/_store/git_locking.py:265-283: `_resolve_common_git_dir` follows the `commondir` pointer away from the per-worktree git dir
findings.finding: The lock scan assumes the reflog and HEAD locks live under the common git dir (top level, refs/, logs/). The repo's own docs say the tickets store is a linked worktree sharing the object DB. In that layout, `git reflog expire --all` writes the worktree's HEAD reflog and its `HEAD.lock` under the per-worktree git dir (`<common>/worktrees/<name>/`), which none of the planned scan paths cover. The only planned test plants `.git/HEAD.lock` in a plain repo, so it cannot catch this.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (lock listing scope); Testing (124 test)
scenarios: On a linked-worktree tickets store, reflog expiry is killed at 30 s while holding `worktrees/<name>/HEAD.lock`. The ERROR lists nothing, and the next write fails on the stranded HEAD lock with no pointer to its location.
findings.suggested_fix: Resolve both `_resolve_tracker_git_dir(tracker)` and `_resolve_common_git_dir(tracker)`. Scan the top level and `logs/` of each, plus `refs/` under the common dir, and remove duplicates when the two dirs are the same.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the 124 lock listing scan both the tracker's per-worktree git dir (StorePaths.git_dir: HEAD.lock, logs/HEAD.lock) and the common dir, searching refs/ and logs/ recursively, and add a linked-worktree variant of the 124 test that plants the per-worktree HEAD.lock.
evidence: Plan: "lists every `*.lock` under the common git dir's top level, `refs/` and `logs/`"
Plan: "a ref lock stranded by the kill blocks writes until removed"
src/rebar/_store/paths.py: StorePaths distinguishes git_dir (per-worktree, `gitdir:` pointer) from git_common_dir
src/rebar/_store/git_locking.py:_resolve_common_git_dir resolves past the per-worktree dir to the common dir
findings.finding: The 124 diagnostic lists `*.lock` only under the common git dir's top level, refs/ and logs/. For a linked-worktree tracker, the per-worktree HEAD and its reflog live in `<common>/worktrees/<name>/`, so a stranded HEAD.lock or logs/HEAD.lock from the killed expiry is never reported. That is the most likely stranded lock, since HEAD's 4.7 MB reflog is the file being rewritten. The planned test plants `.git/HEAD.lock` in a plain repo, so it cannot catch this. The plan also does not say whether nested ref locks (refs/heads/tickets.lock, logs/refs/heads/tickets.lock) are found, i.e. whether the scan is recursive.
findings.location: Approach step 1 (124 ERROR lock listing); Testing ("A 124 test plants `.git/HEAD.lock`")
scenarios: A stalled volume makes the expiry on a linked-worktree tracker hit 30 s. It is killed while holding `<common>/worktrees/<name>/HEAD.lock`. The ERROR names no lock, and every later ticket commit fails until an operator finds the lock by hand.
findings.suggested_fix: Collect lock candidates from StorePaths(tracker).git_dir (top level and logs/) as well as StorePaths(tracker).git_common_dir (top level plus a recursive walk of refs/ and logs/). Add a test case with a linked-worktree tracker that plants `<common>/worktrees/<name>/HEAD.lock` and asserts the ERROR names it.

findings.finding: The runbook's main capability claim, that `git -c pack.threads=1 gc --cruft --prune=2.weeks.ago` removes both expired loose and expired packed unreachable objects while keeping fresh ones, was verified only on git 2.56. The runbook is written to run inside the production MCP container, which the plan itself measured at git 2.47.3. The plan already found one behaviour difference across this exact version gap (maintenance's reflog-expire task), so the runbook claim is unverified on the version it targets.
findings.location: Approach step 2 — infra/runbooks/tickets-store-prune.md ('Verified locally on git 2.56')
scenarios: An operator runs the runbook on 2.47.3. If gc's cruft/prune handling of loose objects differs there, expired loose objects survive. The re-measure step then shows less reclaimed than expected, after a roughly 10-minute write-lock outage.
findings.suggested_fix: Repeat the local 30-day-old loose and packed object experiment with a git 2.47.3 binary (for example, the production container image run locally) and record the result in the runbook. Alternatively, add a precondition step to the runbook: run `git --version`, and stop if it is below the version that was verified.
